claims.text: The investigated material is a quaternary equiatomic FCC solid-solution alloy.
The initial alloy is fully annealed and single phase.
The alloy has high or moderate stacking-fault energy that permits cross-slip while retaining mechanical instability.
At low strain rates, plastic deformation is governed by thermally activated dislocation glide and cross-slip.
Low-strain-rate dislocation plasticity produces positive strain-rate sensitivity.
High strain rates produce stress-induced stacking faults, transient nanotwins, or martensitic nuclei at the yield point.
The proposed stress-induced martensitic transformation converts FCC material to HCP and/or BCC material.
The transformation-related structures impede dislocation motion or absorb deformation energy.
At high strain rates, adiabatic heating and elevated stress trigger the phase transformation.
The transformation supplies a competing, strain-rate-insensitive deformation mode.
Activation of the transformation decouples yield strength from the logarithmic strain-rate dependence associated with dislocation glide.
Yield strength will increase approximately linearly with logarithmic strain rate at low rates and then plateau or saturate above approximately 10^2 s^-1.
The high-rate yield-strength plateau will be accompanied by detectable HCP or BCC phase in the deformed region.
In the absence of phase transformation, standard dislocation-glide behavior predicts a continuous monotonic increase in yield strength with strain rate without saturation.

The proposed transition requires stacking-fault energy within a critical range that permits mechanical instability, whereas sufficiently high stacking-fault energy suppresses twinning or transformation.
The proposed transition requires the test temperature to remain below the critical temperature for reverse transformation.
The critical strain rate for transformation depends strongly on elemental composition and the resulting stacking-fault energy.

contradictions.description: The initial state permits an unspecified 'high' stacking-fault energy while also describing the alloy as mechanically unstable, but the boundary condition states that sufficiently high stacking-fault energy suppresses the twinning or transformation required by the hypothesis. No numerical SFE range resolves this tension.
